name: Piazza and Single House Core
description: The Charleston arrangement: one room wide, turned end-on to the street, with stacked open piazzas along the long southern or western flank and a false street door that opens onto the piazza rather than into the house. A climate machine disguised as a plan, and the most inventive threshold sequence in American architecture.

rooms.note: One per storey, and they are circulation as much as they are outdoor rooms.
The street door in the garden wall.

internal_rules.statement: The piazza faces within 45 degrees of southwest, to catch the prevailing summer breeze and shade the long wall. A piazza on the north flank is decoration and defeats the type.
Piazza depth 10 to 14 ft, at least equal to the depth of an interior room. Below 10 ft it fails as a room and becomes a balcony.
The street door opens onto the piazza, not into the house. Removing this move destroys the type.
Rooms are single-pile so every one is lit and ventilated from two sides, and openings align through the plan for cross draft.
Principal-floor ceiling not less than 11 ft 6 in. Below that the vertical sash proportion and the stack effect both fail.
Superimposed orders on a two-storey piazza: heavier below, lighter above. Identical columns on both levels read as a modern deck.

attaches_to.note: The double-house version, four rooms to a floor, still with the piazza.
Double-pile defeats the cross ventilation the type exists for.

expansion_logic: Lengthen to the rear; the kitchen house stays detached in the yard. The type does not grow forward past the piazza line.
servicing_strategy: Detached kitchen house in the rear yard, joined by a covered way; the piazza carries circulation so interior corridors are unnecessary.

style_variation.note: The type itself. It wears Georgian, Federal and Greek Revival dress in turn without changing plan, section or orientation, which is what makes it a type rather than a style.
The Georgian dress on this core: superimposed Tuscan and Ionic on the piazza, London-quality joinery inside.

sources: Severens, Charleston: Antebellum Architecture and Civic Destiny
